H.G. Wells was a British author and futurist who is considered one of the most influential writers of science fiction. Born in 1866, Wells grew up in a poor family in Kent, England. He became a schoolteacher at the age of 17 and later studied for a degree in biology at the University of London.

Wells published his first science fiction novel, "The Time Machine," in 1895 and soon became one of the most popular writers in the genre. He is best known for his works on the future, including "The War of the Worlds" (1898), "The Time Machine" (1895), "The Island of Dr. Moreau" (1896), and "The Invisible Man" (1897).

Wells was also a prolific writer of short stories and nonfiction, and his work has been translated into more than 30 languages. He was a vocal advocate for progressive causes, including socialism, republicanism, and the rights of working-class people.

Wells died in 1946, but his work continues to be widely read and studied today. He is considered one of the most important and influential writers of science fiction and is often cited as a major influence by other writers in the genre.
